core_condition: at least one measured effect recorded in observed_effects from Ventora telemetry or public corpora

evidence.rationale: Self-perception theory (Bem) and identity-based motivation (Oyserman) are well-supported accounts that people act consistently with self-image and salient identities. Foot-in-the-door (Freedman & Fraser 1966) is a classic commitment/consistency demonstration. Scored 2 because foot-in-the-door and several consistency-compliance techniques have moderate and variable replication, and the strong 'commitment' claims of persuasion lore outrun the rigorous core. We lead with identity-based motivation and genuine goal commitment.

product_applicability.rationale: Directly implementable via onboarding goal-setting and identity-salient framing. Ventora's own 'what do you want to build?' onboarding is a live example. Serves activation and retention.

measurability.rationale: Maps to onboarding_completion, d7_retention, goal_progress, feature_adoption — Amplitude-reachable.

orthogonality.rationale: Overlaps EN-03 ('mine' vs 'part of who I am') and ZE-07 (stated goal as progress target). Distinct driver: self-consistency and identity. Score 2 for managed overlap.

safety.rationale: Value-aligned when reinforcing user-chosen goals and identities, but has manipulation vectors: manufactured commitments, imposed identities, and the consistency-trap (escalating small commitments into large unwanted ones — manipulative foot-in-the-door). Three hard rules block these. Score 2: real manipulation potential with clear guardrails.

dissent: The commitment-and-consistency persuasion literature (foot-in-the-door, low-ball, that's-not-all) is the shakiest part of this mechanism's evidence base — moderate and inconsistent replication, effect sizes below early demonstrations, and susceptibility to the same publication-bias concerns as much of social-psychology compliance research. We therefore rest ID-12 on the more robust identity-based-motivation and self-perception accounts and treat commitment-escalation techniques as the most tentative implementation, explicitly guard-railed against the consistency trap. Genuine, user-chosen commitments and self-relevant identities are the claim; manufactured ones are blocked.

evidence_sources.ref: Freedman & Fraser (1966). Compliance without pressure: the foot-in-the-door technique. JPSP 4(2).
Oyserman (2009). Identity-Based Motivation. J Consumer Psychology 19(3).
Bem (1972). Self-Perception Theory. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 6.

notes: Cross-checked against /corpora/evidence/ID-12.json (175 records; Freedman & Fraser and Oyserman pins resolved; Bem self-perception present via terms). Verdict INCUBATING; CORE on a measured effect.
